title: Not one stone (Mark 13:1–13)
hook: he foretells the temple's fall and hard times: don't be anxious what to say

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow's two coins, and your line was she gave all she had. Who did you tell that you'd noticed? Day two hundred fifteen.

Picture a first-time visitor to a huge city, neck craned back, staring at the skyline. That's one of the disciples as they walk out of the temple. In the King James Bible: "Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!" And he had a point. King Herod had rebuilt the temple on a massive scale, and some of its stones were bigger than a truck. You can still see some of the giant stones of its outer wall in Jerusalem today. And Jesus says: "Seest thou these great buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down." Later they sit on the Mount of Olives, looking across the valley at the temple glowing in the sun, and four of them ask him quietly: when? And how will we know?
screen: `WHAT STONES! WHAT BUILDINGS!` → `NOT ONE STONE UPON ANOTHER.` → `WHEN? HOW WILL WE KNOW?`

segments.voice: What follows is the longest speech Jesus gives in Mark, all of chapter thirteen. Scholars sometimes call it the little apocalypse. It's full of strange images, and Christians read it in several ways; we'll take it in pieces over three days. Today, the beginning. He doesn't give them a date. He gives them warnings. Watch out that no one deceives you. Many will come claiming to be him. You'll hear of wars and rumors of wars; don't be troubled. Earthquakes, famines: these, he says, are the beginnings of sorrows, a word for birth pains. Painful, but not the end. Then it gets personal. You'll be handed over to councils, beaten, brought before governors and kings because of me. Families will split. And right there, in the middle of the frightening part, the most tender line: "take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost." Don't rehearse it. Don't lie awake scripting it. You won't be alone. History adds a hard footnote. In the year 70, during a Jewish revolt, Roman armies destroyed the temple. It has never been rebuilt, and Jews mourn its loss to this day, especially on a fast called Tisha B'Av. Many scholars think Mark was written close to that time. And the section ends: he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. Not the one with the best speech. The one who keeps going.
screen: `NO DATE, JUST WARNINGS.` · `THE BEGINNING OF BIRTH PAINS.` · `DON'T SCRIPT IT BEFOREHAND.` · `THE TEMPLE FELL IN THE YEAR 70.` · then, large: `IT IS NOT YE THAT SPEAK, BUT THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set down one worry about tomorrow. Settle, and breathe. What conversation, meeting or moment are you already rehearsing in your head? The awkward talk, the interview, the appointment. Notice how many times you've played it through. Now picture setting it down, like a heavy bag at the door, just for these two minutes. It'll still be there. You don't have to carry it right now. If you pray, you can hand it to God and trust what will be given in that hour. The bell holds the time.
Not one stone. The temple's great stones would fall. And in hard times: don't worry beforehand what to say.
Your line: don't worry beforehand. Today, when you catch yourself rehearsing tomorrow, stop, breathe, and come back to now. Day two hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Christians facing trials or hard conversations often pray for the Holy Spirit's help in what to say, taking comfort from this promise, and many churches read Mark 13 in Advent.

fork.setup: you're told you'll one day stand before governors and kings because of your faith. what does Jesus tell you to do?
options: don't worry beforehand; say what is given you.
fork.reveal: "take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak ... for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost."

original.note: Greek: worry beforehand. pro, ahead, and merimnaō, to be anxious.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scary prediction about the end of the world.
what it means: warnings, not a timetable; hard times, and a promise not to face them alone.
what a scholar hears: the little apocalypse, birth-pain imagery, the fall of the temple in 70, and promerimnaō, worrying ahead of time.

notes: 'Some of its stones were bigger than a truck': Herodian ashlars in the Western Wall reach roughly 12–13 meters; confirm the comparison.
The Western Wall is part of the temple mount's retaining wall; the script says 'its outer wall'. Confirm phrasing.
Mark's dating near 70 CE is a majority scholarly view, not certain; stated as 'many scholars think'.
Tisha B'Av mention is a brief, respectful neighbor note; Keeper to confirm.
'Mark 13 in Advent' in howItsDone: common in lectionaries (e.g. Year B, First Sunday of Advent reads 13:24–37). Confirm.
